passages.text: Determinants of Frequent Attendance in Primary Care. <sentence_start/>A Systematic Review of Longitudinal Studies

<bold>Introduction:</bold> There is a lack of a systematic review synthesizing longitudinal studies investigating the determinants of frequent attendance in primary care. <sentence_start/>The goal of our systematic review was to fill this gap in knowledge.

<bold>Methods:</bold> Three electronic databases (Medline, PsycINFO, and CINAHL) were searched. <sentence_start/>Longitudinal observational studies analyzing the predictors of frequent attendance in primary care were included. <sentence_start/>Data extraction covered methods, sample characteristics, and main findings. <sentence_start/>Selection of the studies, extracting the data and evaluation of study quality was performed by two reviewers. <sentence_start/>In the results section, the determinants of frequent attendance were presented based on the (extended) Andersen model.

<bold>Results:</bold> In total, 11 longitudinal studies have been included in our systematic review. <sentence_start/>The majority of studies showed that frequent attendance was positively associated with the predisposing characteristics lower age, and unemployment. <sentence_start/>Moreover, it was mainly not associated with enabling resources. <sentence_start/>Most of the studies showed that need factors, and in particular worse self-rated health, lower physical functioning and physical illnesses were associated with an increased likelihood of frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>While most studies were of good quality, several of the included studies did not perform sensitivity analysis or described how they dealt with missing data.

<bold>Discussion:</bold> Our systematic review showed that particularly lower age, unemployment and need factors are associated with the likelihood of becoming a frequent attender. <sentence_start/>Enabling resources are mainly not associated with the outcome measure. <sentence_start/>Future research should concentrate on the determinants of persistent frequent attendance due to the high economic burden associated with it.
Introduction

Primary health care can be defined as an “approach to health and a spectrum of services beyond the traditional health care system. <sentence_start/>It includes all services that play a part in health, such as income, housing, education, and environment.” <sentence_start/>Primary care is an “element within primary health care that focuses on health care services, including health promotion, illness and injury prevention, and the diagnosis and treatment of illness and injury” (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF03405354" pmid="17120883" pmcid="PMC6976192" count="1">1</citation>). <sentence_start/>A quite small proportion of patients typically cause a considerable proportion of visits in primary care (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-016-1357-y" pmid="27074709" pmcid="PMC4831189" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consequently, frequent attendance (synonymously, high utilization or heavy use) in primary care is associated with high costs (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/archpsyc.1992.01820020011002" pmid="1550468" count="1">3</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the same vein, frequent attendance is also associated with future sick leave days and illness-based retirement (disability pensions) (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1403494819838663" pmid="30973068" pmcid="PMC7042497" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, it should be noted that frequent attendance can cause frustration, stress and burnout among physicians (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9604412" pmcid="PMC1409909" count="1">5</citation>-<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.puhe.2004.03.007" pmid="15694959" count="1">8</citation>)-which is important for its own sake and, additionally, these factors can also have an impact on patient and doctor satisfaction (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/archinte.159.10.1069" pmid="10335683" count="1">9</citation>-<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/fampra/19.2.178" pmid="11906984" count="1">13</citation>).

The factors associated with frequent attendance in primary care have often been studied based on cross-sectional data [e.g., (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s40520-020-01495-2" pmid="32108287" count="1">14</citation>-<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5455/msm.2019.31.93-98" pmid="31452632" pmcid="PMC6690307" count="1">20</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>An existing systematic review (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12875-017-0700-7" pmid="29262771" pmcid="PMC5738881" count="1">21</citation>) examined the correlates of frequent attendance in European countries. <sentence_start/>They performed a literature search in November 2016 and mainly identified cross-sectional studies, whereas only one longitudinal study was identified. <sentence_start/>In total, they particularly found a link between increased need (for example, worse self-rated health or more chronic conditions) and an increased likelihood of being a frequent attender. <sentence_start/>They also concluded that longitudinal studies are necessary to determine the factors which can contribute to frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>Actually, in the last years, some longitudinal studies have been published in peer-reviewed journals [for example (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.healthpol.2018.03.014" pmid="29631780" count="1">26</citation>)].

More generally, longitudinal studies are needed to improve our understanding of the factors that may contribute to frequent attendance in primary care. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, there is a lack of studies systematically synthesizing longitudinal studies which analyzed the determinants of frequent attendance in primary care. <sentence_start/>Hence, our goal was to provide an overview of the existing longitudinal observational studies investigating the determinants of frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>Knowledge about the determinants may assist in managing health care use in primary care and might help in decreasing the economic costs linked to heavy or excessive use of primary care (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3205/psm000089" pmid="23133505" pmcid="PMC3488807" count="1">27</citation>, <citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2019.1673310" pmid="31591911" count="1">28</citation>).

It is worth noting that the determinants of health care use (HCU; including frequent attendance) have often been examined based on the Andersen model of health care utilization (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2307/2137284" pmid="7738325" count="1">29</citation>) which distinguishes between predisposing characteristics like age or sex, enabling resources like income or access to primary care and need factors like self-rated health or chronic illnesses. <sentence_start/>Moreover, it has recently been proposed to extend the Andersen model by including psychosocial factors like loneliness or personality factors like neuroticism in the Andersen model (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3399/bjgpopen20X101088" pmid="32430301" pmcid="PMC7330227" count="1">30</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, the determinants of frequent attendance are presented based on the Andersen model in our results section.
Methods

We conducted our systematic review in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis guidelines (<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.g7647" pmid="25555855" count="1">31</citation>). <sentence_start/>Our systematic review is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, registration number: CRD42020178077). <sentence_start/>Moreover, a study protocol for our systematic review has recently been published (<citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph17103710" pmid="32466103" pmcid="PMC7277920" count="1">32</citation>).
Search Strategy and Selection Criteria

A systematic literature search was performed in June 2020. <sentence_start/>To this end, three databases were searched (Medline, PsycINFO, and CINAHL). <sentence_start/>The search query for Medline is shown in Table 1.

Using a two-step process (independently conducted by two reviewers, AH and BK), studies were assessed for inclusion/exclusion: (i) Title/abstract screening and (ii) Full-text screening. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the reference lists of the finally included articles were hand searched (i.e., backwards- and forwards- citation analysis) by both reviewers. <sentence_start/>In case of disagreements, discussions were used to resolve it (or by including a third party, HHK).

Our inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Observational longitudinal studies analyzing the factors associated with frequent attendance in primary care in any age group, (2) studies adequately quantifying frequent attendance in primary care, and (3) studies published in peer-reviewed journals in English or German language. <sentence_start/>Exclusion criteria were: (1) cross-sectional observational studies, (2) studies solely investigating samples with specific disorders, (3) not an observational study, (4) inappropriate measurement of frequent attendance like an uncertain period for frequent attendance, and (5) studies not published in a peer-reviewed journal or in language other than German or English.

We did not apply restrictions with regard to location or time of the studies. <sentence_start/>Prior to final eligibility criteria, we conducted a pre-test (with a sample of 100 titles/abstracts), though eligibility criteria did not change.
Data Extraction and Analysis

Data extraction was performed by one reviewer (BK) and a cross-check was performed by a second reviewer (AH). <sentence_start/>In case of disagreement, discussions were held to reach a consensus (or by inclusion of a third party, HHK). <sentence_start/>If clarification was required, the study authors were contacted.

We extracted data on study design, assessment of frequent attendance, sample characteristics, sample size, and main findings regarding the determinants of frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>We present the main findings based on the Andersen model of health care use.
Quality Assessment

First, it should be emphasized that a consensus on a quality assessment tool for HCU studies does not exist [see also (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/healthcare8030329" pmid="32806553" pmcid="PMC7551013" count="1">33</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>Consequently, we used a tool created by Stuhldreher et al. (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/eat.20977" pmid="22294558" count="1">34</citation>) and improved by Hohls et al. (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jad.2018.02.011" pmid="29494900" count="1">35</citation>). <sentence_start/>This tool was also used in former studies [e.g., (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/healthcare8030329" pmid="32806553" pmcid="PMC7551013" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jad.2018.02.011" pmid="29494900" count="1">35</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>For further details, please see Table 2. <sentence_start/>Two reviewers (AH and BK) conducted the quality assessment. <sentence_start/>If required, discussions were held to reach a consensus or by inclusion of a third party (HHK).
Results
Overview of Included Studies

In Figure 1, the study selection process is shown (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pmed.1000097" pmid="19621072" pmcid="PMC2707599" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>In sum, <italic>n</italic> = 11 studies are included in the final synthesis of our review. <sentence_start/>In Table 3, key characteristics and main findings of the studies are presented (if reported, adjusted results are presented).
Figure 1
PRISMA flow diagram.

Data came from Asia (<italic>n</italic> = 1, Oman), Europe (<italic>n</italic> = 7, with three studies from Germany, two studies from the United Kingdom, one study from Slovenia, and one study from Finland), and three studies from Australia (<italic>n</italic> = 3, all from the country Australia). <sentence_start/>The period of observation in the included longitudinal studies ranged from 4 months to 12 years.

The majority (<italic>n</italic> = 7) of studies used the highest decile (in terms of frequency of GP visits) as cut-off for being a frequent attender (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>-<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.healthpol.2018.03.014" pmid="29631780" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12889-018-6217-8" pmid="30477466" pmcid="PMC6260555" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, while two studies used twelve or more GP visits in the study year as cut-off (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5001/omj.2018.60" pmid="30038733" pmcid="PMC6047176" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/abm/kax054" pmid="30212847" count="1">38</citation>), a third study used eight visits as cut-off [= top quartile (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0033291711001589" pmid="21880165" count="1">41</citation>)] and a fourth study used six visits as cut-off (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>). <sentence_start/>While some studies used the self-reported frequency of GP visits [e.g., (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>)], other studies used administrative data [e.g., (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.healthpol.2018.03.014" pmid="29631780" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12889-018-6217-8" pmid="30477466" pmcid="PMC6260555" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>For example, one study extracted the number of visits from the electronic medical records system in Oman (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5001/omj.2018.60" pmid="30038733" pmcid="PMC6047176" count="1">37</citation>).

While most of the studies broadly examined the determinants of temporary or persistent frequent attendance, for instance, one study focused on the link between insecure attachment and frequent attendance (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0033291711001589" pmid="21880165" count="1">41</citation>), another study concentrated on the link between out-of-pocket costs and frequent attendance (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.healthpol.2018.03.014" pmid="29631780" count="1">26</citation>) and a further study concentrated on the link between aging satisfaction and frequent attendance (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, it should be noted that some of the studies included focused on temporary frequent attendance [like (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>)], whereas other studies (also) examined persistent frequent attendance [e.g., (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>)].

The majority of the studies focused on middle-aged or older individuals. <sentence_start/>The proportion of women mainly ranged from about 50-70%, with a sample size ranging from 79 to 66,831 individuals. <sentence_start/>In Table 3, further details are shown. <sentence_start/>Despite the fact that only three out (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>) of eleven studies included in our review used the Andersen model as theoretical background, we will present our main findings in the following sections according to the [extended (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3399/bjgpopen20X101088" pmid="32430301" pmcid="PMC7330227" count="1">30</citation>)] Andersen model (to increase readability and clarity): predisposing characteristics, enabling resources, need factors and psychosocial factors.
Predisposing Characteristics

In total, <italic>n</italic> = 7 studies explicitly examined the link between predisposing characteristics (including age, sex and employment status) and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>It should be noted that not all seven studies included all of the aforementioned predisposing characteristics.

With regard to age, while one study did not identify a link between age and frequent attendance (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>), a second study found a bivariate association between higher age and an increased likelihood of frequent attendance (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5001/omj.2018.60" pmid="30038733" pmcid="PMC6047176" count="1">37</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, studies based on nationally representative samples and using advanced techniques like FE regressions found a robust link between increased age and a lower probability of becoming a frequent attender in Germany (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>).

With regard to sex, there is inconclusive evidence. <sentence_start/>For example, while one study found a link between being female and an increased likelihood of being a frequent attender (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>), another study mainly did not identify such a link (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>). <sentence_start/>Other studies used sex-stratified regressions [e.g., (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>)] or used FE regression techniques [e.g., (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>In these FE regression models, time-constant factors (i.e., factors that do not vary within individuals over time) like sex can only be included as moderating factors. <sentence_start/>One study (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>) examined whether time-constant factors like sex or educational level moderate the link between need factors (in terms of chronic conditions, physical functioning, self-rated health and depression) and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>However, all of the respective interaction terms did not achieve statistical significance. <sentence_start/>In this context, it may be worth noting that one study found a link between lower educational level and an increased likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>), whereas the majority of studies included did not investigate this factor.

With regard to employment status, while some single studies did not find an association between unemployment and becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>), most of the studies found a link between unemployment and an increased likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>).

While only one single study (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>) found a link between getting married and an increased likelihood of frequent attendance, other studies did not identify such a link (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>, <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>).
Enabling Resources

In sum, <italic>n</italic> = 6 studies examined the association between enabling resources and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>One study found a link between financial pressure and an increased likelihood of being a frequent attender (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, studies relying on more advanced panel techniques consistently did not determine a link between income or financial pressure and the likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, a further study did not find a link between out-of-pocket costs and frequent attendance using a counterfactual model adjusting for selection into cost levels (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.healthpol.2018.03.014" pmid="29631780" count="1">26</citation>).
Need Factors

In total, <italic>n</italic> = 7 studies examined the association between need factors and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>They almost consistently found a link between increased need factors and an increased likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12889-018-6217-8" pmid="30477466" pmcid="PMC6260555" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>). <sentence_start/>More precisely, particularly self-rated health, physical functioning and physical illnesses were quite strongly associated with frequent attendance (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12889-018-6217-8" pmid="30477466" pmcid="PMC6260555" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>).

There is mixed evidence regarding mental health and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>For example, while some studies identified a link between mental health, depression, or anxiety and an increased likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>), other studies did not find a significant link (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>-<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>).

It may be worth noting that two studies identified a link between increased medication use (e.g., for sleep problems or high blood pressure) and an increased likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>). <sentence_start/>A further study did not identify an association between cognitive functioning and frequent attendance in primary care (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>).
Psychosocial Factors

In total, <italic>n</italic> = 3 studies examined the link between psychosocial factors and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>However, these studies largely differed in the key independent variables. <sentence_start/>For example, one recent study showed a link between increased self-perceptions of aging and a decreased likelihood of becoming a frequent attender (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another study revealed that frequent attendance was significantly related to insecure emotional attachment style (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0033291711001589" pmid="21880165" count="1">41</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, another study showed that loneliness is not associated with frequent attendance in primary care longitudinally (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>).
Quality Assessment

In Table 4, the quality assessment of studies included in our systematic review is shown. <sentence_start/>In sum, 81.3-93.8% of the criteria were met by the longitudinal studies included in our review. <sentence_start/>By far, the categories with the most unmet criteria were how missing data were handled (9% fulfilled) and whether sensitivity analyses were performed (45% fulfilled).
Discussion
The aim of this systematic review was to provide an overview of the existing longitudinal observational studies investigating the determinants of frequent attendance.

With regard to <italic>predisposing characteristics</italic>, only lower age and (to a lesser degree) unemployment were almost consistently associated with a higher likelihood of becoming a frequent attender, whereas there is rather inconclusive evidence regarding sex, educational level and marital status. <sentence_start/>At first glance, the link between age and frequent attendance may appear counterintuitive. <sentence_start/>However, a possible link may be that with increasing age individuals become less optimistic about the treatment or may have increased perceived opportunity costs with regard to physician visits (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, the link between a job loss and frequent attendance may be driven by changes in health behavior associated with unemployment (<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/eurpub/8.1.21" count="1">43</citation>). <sentence_start/>In conclusion, only some predisposing characteristics were consistently associated with frequent attendance, whereas there is inconclusive evidence regarding several predisposing characteristics. <sentence_start/>Future longitudinal studies are required to shed more light on these factors.

With regard to <italic>enabling resources</italic>, existing studies almost consistently did not determine an association between enabling resources (like income) and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>These findings may be mainly driven by the characteristics of the health insurance systems of the included studies. <sentence_start/>Thus, future research, particularly from countries where the ownership of the healthcare system is mainly in private hands (e.g., United States) is required because enabling resources commonly play a key role in these countries. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, future studies are necessary to examine the link between (perceived) access to primary care and frequent attendance.

With regard to <italic>need factors</italic>, most of the included longitudinal studies found an association between need factors (particularly physical functioning, and physical illnesses) and frequent attendance (both, temporary and persistent). <sentence_start/>This is highly plausible and in line with various cross-sectional studies (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12875-017-0700-7" pmid="29262771" pmcid="PMC5738881" count="1">21</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, it should be noted that various studies did not show a link between depression and frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>This may be explained by the fact that individuals with depression are often referred to the specialist. <sentence_start/>In total, these findings may indicate that patients mainly have frequent primary care visits when medically indicated. <sentence_start/>More research is required to examine the link between specific diseases or disease clusters and frequent attendance longitudinally. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, longitudinal studies focusing on the link between functional complaints (i.e., medically unexplained symptoms) and frequent attendance in primary care are required (<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1017/S0033291711001589" pmid="21880165" count="1">41</citation>, <citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2458-9-36" pmid="19166622" pmcid="PMC2649070" count="1">44</citation>). <sentence_start/>For example, it has been shown that frequent attenders with medically unexplained symptoms have an increased use and increased costs of medical investigations (<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1192/bjp.180.3.248" pmid="11872517" count="1">45</citation>).

With regard to <italic>psychosocial factors</italic>, only some single studies exist which largely differed in their key independent variables. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we refrained from drawing conclusions from these single studies. <sentence_start/>It should be emphasized and repeated that while most of the included studies focused on rather conventional explanatory variables like sex, age or health-related factors, psychosocial factors like loneliness or satisfaction have rarely been examined. <sentence_start/>Since, for example, a recent cross-sectional study has demonstrated that after adjusting for various covariates, psychosocial factors are still important determinants of frequent attendance (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12875-017-0621-5" pmid="28340559" pmcid="PMC5366110" count="1">16</citation>), we hope that future longitudinal studies close this gap in knowledge. <sentence_start/>Moreover, it has been demonstrated that personality factors like neuroticism are important for health care use (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/healthcare8030329" pmid="32806553" pmcid="PMC7551013" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1468-0009.12024" pmid="24028697" pmcid="PMC3790523" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/bjhp.12236" pmid="28345258" count="1">47</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, personality-related factors like external health locus of control (i.e., the belief that health depends on others like GPs) may heavily drive frequent attendance in primary care (<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/bjhp.12236" pmid="28345258" count="1">47</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, factors such as increased health anxiety may be of importance for an increased likelihood of being a frequent attender (<citation rid="B48" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11766871" pmcid="PMC1314191" count="1">48</citation>, <citation rid="B49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/fampra/cmv076" pmid="26450918" pmcid="PMC5926457" count="1">49</citation>). <sentence_start/>Therefore, we also hope that future research will shed light onto the link between personality factors (in a broader sense) and frequent attendance.

Against this backdrop, the importance of the conventional Andersen model as a theoretical foundation for analyzing the determinants of frequent attendance in primary care can be critically discussed. <sentence_start/>However, we think that this extended version (including psychosocial and personality-related factors) offers a promising theoretical framework in this context (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3399/bjgpopen20X101088" pmid="32430301" pmcid="PMC7330227" count="1">30</citation>).

The variety in study quality between the studies was rather low and, in general, the study quality of the included studies was rather high. <sentence_start/>The general high quality is rather unsurprising given the fact that all studies have been published in the last 10 years. <sentence_start/>However, common shortcomings of the included studies are that more than one half of studies included did not perform sensitivity analysis. <sentence_start/>This is, however, of importance to verify the robustness of the study findings and current guidelines therefore recommend these robustness checks (<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijsu.2014.07.013" pmid="25046131" count="1">50</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, only one study described how missing data were handled. <sentence_start/>This can result in, among other things, biased parameter estimates, biased standard error estimates or a severe loss of statistical power (<citation rid="B51" ref-type="bibr" count="1">51</citation>). <sentence_start/>Future studies should overcome this limitation [e.g., by using techniques such as full-information maximum likelihood (<citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/10705511.2015.1047931" count="1">52</citation>)] because these missing-data techniques may result in more accurate and reliable results (<citation rid="B51" ref-type="bibr" count="1">51</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, only three studies used the Andersen model as theoretical background and for selection of independent variables. <sentence_start/>However, in total, we cautiously assume that these shortcomings (i.e., how missing data were handled and absence of sensitivity analysis) did not heavily affect the robustness of our review's findings. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, we cannot dismiss the possibility of a publication bias. <sentence_start/>Moreover, future research is required to clarify how exactly these shortcomings regarding missing data and sensitivity analysis can affect the robustness of systematic reviews.

In total, and related to the quality of the studies, there are some factors that restrict the comparability of the studies included in our review. <sentence_start/>While some studies are based on individuals recruited in general practices, other studies used data from region-wide (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>, <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.healthpol.2018.03.014" pmid="29631780" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>) or nationally representative (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>) samples. <sentence_start/>Moreover, one study used a random and representative sample of Slovenian family medicine practices' attenders (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>). <sentence_start/>While most of the studies used the highest decile to define frequent attenders, some other studies used cut-offs like at least 12 visits per year (i.e., on average one visit per month). <sentence_start/>Despite using longitudinal data, only a few studies used regression models specifically designed for longitudinal data (like conditional FE logistic regressions) [for example (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>-<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>However, using these regression techniques is important to deliver consistent estimates (<citation rid="B53" ref-type="bibr" count="1">53</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, the question remains whether all of the studies included in our systematic review produced consistent estimates and their findings should be therefore interpreted with caution. <sentence_start/>However, it should be noted that the included studies mostly produced similar results (in terms of direction and significance). <sentence_start/>Moreover, exclusively focusing on studies using panel regression techniques (with conservative model assumptions) supported our main conclusions (i.e., particularly increased needs are associated with becoming a frequent attender).

Included studies partially used self-reported doctor visits. <sentence_start/>This, however, may introduce some bias (recall bias) (<citation rid="B54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1077558705285298" pmid="16595412" count="1">54</citation>). <sentence_start/>Upcoming research should link survey data with claims data (if data are available) to reduce this potential threat to the validity. <sentence_start/>As noted above, existing studies focused on a variety of explanatory variables. <sentence_start/>For instance, while one study focused on aging satisfaction as explanatory variable (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>), other studies [e.g., (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph16091553" pmid="31052591" pmcid="PMC6539949" count="1">22</citation>, <citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-018-3487-x" pmid="30165847" pmcid="PMC6117977" count="1">23</citation>)] focused on common explanatory variables based on the Andersen model. <sentence_start/>Moreover, while some studies focused on temporary frequent attendance, other studies (also) concentrated on persistent frequent attenders [e.g., (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0054241" pmid="23342107" pmcid="PMC3546928" count="1">40</citation>, <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008975" pmid="26443661" pmcid="PMC4606421" count="1">42</citation>)] as outcome measure. <sentence_start/>Studies also exist mainly focusing on persistent frequent attenders (<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2458-9-36" pmid="19166622" pmcid="PMC2649070" count="1">44</citation>, <citation rid="B55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3399/bjgp09X395120" pmid="19192367" pmcid="PMC2629841" count="1">55</citation>-<citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0073125" pmid="24039870" pmcid="PMC3764153" count="1">57</citation>). <sentence_start/>For instance, it has been shown that among 1 year frequent attenders, about one out of six became a persistent frequent attender (<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2458-9-36" pmid="19166622" pmcid="PMC2649070" count="1">44</citation>). <sentence_start/>Furthermore, it should be noted that the existing studies focused on patient characteristics, but not on GP- (including GP-patient relationship) (<citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1472-6963-8-178" pmid="18715502" pmcid="PMC2533311" count="1">58</citation>, <citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5694/j.1326-5377.2008.tb01986.x" pmid="18707566" count="1">59</citation>) or system-related characteristics (<citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1503/cmaj.050584" pmid="16415462" pmcid="PMC1329455" count="1">60</citation>). <sentence_start/>These factors may also drive frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>For instance, a cross-sectional study conducted in Slovenia showed a link between higher satisfaction with the family physician and frequent attendance (<citation rid="B61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/028134301316982405" pmid="11697559" count="1">61</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, factors such as collusion (acquiescence by doctor to explanation provided by patient) (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.318.7180.372" pmid="9933202" pmcid="PMC27727" count="1">12</citation>, <citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pec.2007.03.008" pmid="17428634" count="1">62</citation>) which can contribute to questioning of doctor's openness and competence (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.318.7180.372" pmid="9933202" pmcid="PMC27727" count="1">12</citation>) may ultimately affect the likelihood of frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>However, further research is required the longitudinal association between GP-/system-related characteristics and frequent attendance in primary care.

Our systematic review also has some strengths and limitations. <sentence_start/>First, this current work is the first one systematically synthesizing evidence regarding the determinants of frequent attendance in primary care solely concentrating on longitudinal studies. <sentence_start/>Due to the focus on longitudinal studies, we are quite confident that the studies included have a rather high quality and may provide more valid conclusions regarding factors that can affect frequent attendance. <sentence_start/>Moreover, a quality assessment was performed. <sentence_start/>Two reviewers performed main steps like selection of the studies, data extraction and evaluation of study quality. <sentence_start/>A meta-analysis could not be performed because of the heterogeneity between the studies. <sentence_start/>Moreover, we restricted our search to peer-reviewed articles. <sentence_start/>On the one side, this may ascertain a high quality. <sentence_start/>On the other side, we cannot fully dismiss the possibility that some previous findings (e.g., gray literature or conference abstracts) may be missing. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, publications in German and English language were included. <sentence_start/>Again, some studies published in other languages may not be identified in our systematic review. <sentence_start/>Additionally, our search strategy focused on 16 search procedures. <sentence_start/>Our search strategy was, among other things, informed by frequently used keywords of relevant articles [such as (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpsychores.2015.10.007" pmid="26526498" count="1">25</citation>) or (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/13607863.2020.1742659" pmid="32189524" count="1">24</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>However, it should be noted that other terms (e.g., related to help seeking) were not included and we restricted our search to studies including the term “longitudinal”. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, we assume that our systematic review includes at least most of the studies important to our topic since two reviewers additionally performed a hand search of relevant studies (backwards- and forwards- citation tracking).
Conclusions

Our systematic review showed that particularly lower age and need factors (thereof, particularly physical functioning and physical illnesses) are associated with the likelihood of becoming a frequent attender. <sentence_start/>Enabling resources are mainly not associated with the outcome measure. <sentence_start/>Future research should concentrate on the determinants of persistent frequent attendance due to the high economic burden associated with it. <sentence_start/>This may assist in mitigating these costs. <sentence_start/>Moreover, most of the studies included used data from European countries. <sentence_start/>Future research is required from other regions (e.g., African or Asian countries).
